metadata.title: Faster Fluid, Lower Pressure: Bernoulli's Principle
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: When water speeds up through a narrow pipe, does its pressure rise or fall?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: Water flows steadily through a level pipe. Intuition suggests that faster moving fluid should push harder on the walls around it. So when the flow speeds up, does the pressure rise, or fall?
beats.new_visual_element: Horizontal pipe of uniform width filled with light-blue water; rows of small blue tracer dots stream left to right along straight, parallel streamlines. Three pressure gauges (dials on short stems) sit on top of the pipe, all reading the same.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: uniform pipe, steady laminar flow, three equal gauges

beats.narration_text: Now narrow the middle of the pipe. The water is incompressible, so the same volume must pass every cross section each second: A one v one equals A two v two. In the narrow neck, the water must move faster.
beats.new_visual_element: The pipe walls smoothly pinch into a narrow neck; streamlines converge and the tracer dots visibly speed up through the neck. Velocity arrows below the pipe: short v_1 at the wide sections, long v_2 at the neck. Equation A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: necked pipe, faster dots in neck, v_1 / v_2 arrows, continuity equation, gauges still equal

beats.narration_text: To speed up as it enters the neck, each small volume of water needs a net forward force. That force comes from a pressure difference: the pressure behind it must be higher than the pressure ahead. So the pressure in the neck is lower, and it rises again as the pipe widens.
beats.new_visual_element: Gauges labeled p_1, p_2, p_1. The neck gauge's needle sweeps down to a low reading while the outer two stay high. Equation p_2 < p_1.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: necked pipe with flow, v arrows, neck gauge low, outer gauges high, p_2 < p_1

beats.narration_text: Bernoulli's equation makes this an energy statement. For level, frictionless flow of an incompressible fluid, p plus one half rho v squared is the same at every point along a streamline. Where the kinetic energy per unit volume grows, the pressure falls by exactly the same amount.
beats.new_visual_element: Under each gauge, a stacked bar: teal p segment below, gold one-half rho v squared segment above, inside a dotted outline of constant total height. The neck bar's segments re-balance (ReplacementTransform): gold grows, teal shrinks, total unchanged. Equation p + ½ρv² = constant.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: necked pipe with flow, gauges, three stacked energy bars of equal total, Bernoulli equation

beats.narration_text: Faster flow means lower pressure, not higher. Speed and pressure are two parts of one conserved quantity, traded one for the other as the fluid moves along.
beats.new_visual_element: Held frame with the flow still running; a soft gold highlight on the neck and summary line 'FASTER FLOW, LOWER PRESSURE'.
